query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Subjecting non-equilibrium, as-cast Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys to an aging/annealing treatment will promote phase separation, leading to the formation of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds. These intermetallic regions act as preferential sites for Mg oxidation during high-temperature exposure, resulting in a more protective MgO scale, while simultaneously creating local galvanic cells that accelerate pitting corrosion in aggressive environments.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast, non-equilibrium, metastable single-phase Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy with a density below 6 g/cm³.
generation.intervention: Aging/annealing heat treatment designed to induce phase separation.
generation.conditions: Exposure to high-temperature oxidative environments (e.g., elevated temperatures in air) and corrosive conditions (e.g., chloride-containing aqueous solutions) under controlled comparison.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds that nucleate the development of a MgO scale.
generation.mechanism: During the aging/annealing treatment, Mg diffuses to form discrete intermetallic precipitates. Under high-temperature oxidation, these Mg-rich regions preferentially oxidize to form a continuous MgO scale, enhancing oxidation resistance. However, the chemical inhomogeneity established by these intermetallic regions creates localized galvanic cells when exposed to corrosive environments, thereby accelerating pitting corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-cast baseline, the heat-treated alloy will exhibit improved high-temperature oxidation resistance due to the formation of a protective MgO layer, but it will also show an increased tendency for localized corrosion due to galvanic effects at the interfaces between the Mg-rich intermetallic compounds and the surrounding matrix.
generation.baseline: The as-cast, metastable single-phase alloy without significant Mg-rich intermetallic segregation.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys with densities below 6 g/cm³ that are processed to a non-equilibrium state; results may differ for alloys with substantially different compositions or processing histories.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of phase separation and the balance between improved oxidation resistance and accelerated corrosion are not fully determined and may vary with specific alloy compositions and processing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy samples: one set in the as-cast, metastable state and the other subjected to a controlled aging/annealing treatment. Expose both sets to high-temperature oxidation conditions (e.g., at 800°C in air) and to a standardized corrosive environment (e.g., 3.5% NaCl aqueous solution) at room temperature. Analyze phase evolution, oxide scale formation, and corrosion behavior using appropriate characterization techniques.
measurements: Phase identification and quantification of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds (using XRD and SEM-EDS)
Continuity and thickness of the MgO scale (using TEM or surface profiling methods)
Oxidation kinetics (via weight gain measurements over time)
Corrosion performance metrics such as pitting density and corrosion potential (using electrochemical techniques like potentiodynamic polarization and EIS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged/annealed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in high-temperature oxidation resistance or do not show increased localized corrosion (as indicated by pitting density or shifts in corrosion potential) relative to the as-cast baseline, then the mechanistic hypothesis would be considered falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Non‐equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight HEAs evolve during post‐processing (or service at elevated temperatures) via phase decomposition in which the homogeneous, metastable solid solution segregates into Mg‐rich intermetallic compounds. These intermetallic regions serve as preferential sites for Mg oxidation, leading to the in situ formation of a continuous, protective MgO layer during high‐temperature exposure. However, the chemical inhomogeneity introduced by these intermetallics creates local galvanic couples that accelerate localized (pitting) corrosion in corrosive environments compared with the as-cast, more uniform microstructure.
drafts.material_initial_state: As-cast, non-equilibrium, metastable solid solution of a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy with density below 6 g/cm³.
drafts.intervention: Subjecting the alloy to an aging/annealing heat treatment (or simulated high-temperature service conditions) that promotes phase separation.
drafts.conditions: High-temperature oxidative environment for oxidation studies and an aggressive (e.g., chloride-containing) corrosive environment at room or moderate temperature for corrosion studies.
drafts.structural_mediator: Formation of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds that serve as nucleation sites for MgO layer development.
drafts.mechanism: During aging/annealing, diffusion of Mg leads to phase separation from the metastable solid solution, forming discrete Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates. Under high-temperature oxidation conditions, these Mg-rich regions preferentially oxidize, generating a protective MgO scale that improves oxidation resistance. Concurrently, the chemical inhomogeneity with distinct electrochemical potentials between the intermetallic and surrounding matrix establishes localized galvanic cells, thereby accelerating pitting corrosion.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-cast baseline, the heat-treated alloy will exhibit enhanced high-temperature oxidation resistance (due to the formation of a coherent, protective MgO layer) but will show an increased susceptibility to localized corrosion (due to galvanic effects at the intermetallic–matrix interfaces).
drafts.baseline: The as-cast, metastable single-phase solid solution that does not yet exhibit significant Mg-rich intermetallic segregation.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis applies to Mg-containing lightweight HEAs with densities below 6 g/cm³ that are processed to a non-equilibrium state; results might differ outside these composition or processing constraints.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the same Mg-containing lightweight HEA: one set as-cast (metastable state) and one set subjected to controlled aging/annealing treatment. Expose both sets to identical high-temperature oxidation conditions (e.g., 800°C in air) and to a standardized corrosive environment (e.g., 3.5% NaCl aqueous solution) at room temperature. Characterize the phase evolution via XRD and SEM-EDS, measure the scale formation by weight gain and surface analysis, and assess corrosion performance through electrochemical measurements (potentiodynamic polarization and EIS).
measurements: Phase fraction and distribution of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds (via XRD, SEM-EDS)
Thickness and continuity of the MgO scale (via TEM or surface profiling)
Corrosion rate/pitting density and onset potential (via electrochemical tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged/annealed samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in high-temperature oxidation resistance or do not exhibit increased localized corrosion relative to the as-cast samples, then the hypothesis—that phase decomposition and resultant MgO scale development in Mg-rich intermetallic regions drives the observed changes—would be falsified.
